name: Dana Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Dana, thanks for making time. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. It's all confidential. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Wren Hollow, a community-supported farm, which means about two hundred local households pay up front each year for a weekly box. We grow vegetables, keep thirty dairy goats and some laying hens, and there's a ten-acre wheat field we share with a neighbour. I milk the goats at six, then weed, harvest and pack boxes, and I'm honestly still clumsy at most of it. I spent thirty years in the council planning office, so my hands are slower than my head.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you fit into the farm, as the newer one?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ines, the grower who runs it, teaches me the soil and the animals, and I quietly sort out the planning side for her. I use an AI assistant every day, to draft the box newsletter, plan which beds get sown when, and keep the goat milk records tidy. My partner Sam is a social worker, and our kids Mia and Felix are grown and gone. I took the council's early retirement deal, so the farm wage is a bonus, and a decent one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit disappointing. I'd been hoping these tools would get much better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools were useful but oversold, which is true of most things. At the farm's members' evening I'd still show people how I plan the beds with AI, because it saves Ines hours. I'd post a short how-to on the members' group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes almost nothing, which is fine. The weeding is still my back and my knees. I'd keep getting slowly better at the goats and keep handling the computer bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the assistant for the newsletter and the sowing plan, and maybe try one for spotting goat lameness from phone videos. I'd keep my shifts at three and a half days. I'd spend some savings on a polytunnel at home, just for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a touch bored by the anticlimax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your work or money that worries you, even in this flat picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, my council pension is small but safe, and Sam works. Mostly I worry about my own clumsiness. Last week a goat called Pepper kicked the milk bucket across the parlour, and I was more upset about that than about any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the AI saves Ines hours. Does that ever make you feel your own job is less needed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the opposite, it means Ines can spend more time teaching me. The hours it saves are the boring ones. The goats still need someone at six.

I'd still show members how I **plan beds with AI** at the members' evening.
think: Weeding is still **my back and knees**, so little changes.
I'll keep improving with the **goats** and handling the computer side.
do: Try an app for **spotting lameness** from phone videos.
Keep my **usual shifts** at three and a half days, and build a polytunnel at home.
feel: **Calm**, with a touch of **boredom** at the anticlimax.

fieldNote: She is the farm's **quiet planner**, using AI daily despite being junior.

steps.text: Keep using the AI assistant for the box newsletter and sowing plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds like what I expected. And mostly good for somewhere like Wren Hollow, if we're smart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small farms should grab the planning tools now, before the big agribusinesses lock them up behind subscriptions. I'd say it at the members' evening and online. And I'd say people losing office jobs need public retraining, not a pat on the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, it's good news. My job is hands-on, and the thinking tasks on the card are the ones I already hand to the computer. I'd become more useful to Ines, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up an AI ordering system for seeds and feed, so Ines stops forgetting the goat minerals. I'd push the farm to trial a small solar weeding robot that a co-op near us rents out. I'd get our members' group to back a public retraining scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. It's the first time my office years and my farm years fit together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My old colleagues in the planning office, honestly, because checking forms is exactly what the card describes. And Mia, who handles insurance claims all day. My old desk at the council checked planning forms for thirty years, and a computer could do that whole job by lunchtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the weeding robot. Wouldn't that take the weeding you do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it, yes, and good riddance to my knees. There's always more to do on a small farm than hands to do it. I'd rather spend the time on the goats.

People losing office jobs need **public retraining**, not sympathy.

Get members to back a **retraining scheme**.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited** that her two careers fit together.

fieldNote: She reads the change as **good for her**, since her thinking skills complement farm work.
Her concern goes to **ex-colleagues** and to Mia's claims job.
She welcomes automating **weeding**, the task hardest on her body.

steps.text: Set up an AI ordering system for seeds, feed and goat minerals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking part, five for robots. That's quick, even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the robots have to be owned in common, by co-ops and communities, or a few companies end up owning all food. I'd campaign for that loudly. I'd also say a basic income isn't a fantasy any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thinking side in 2028 just makes me more useful. The worry is 2031, when a robot can milk goats and pack boxes. I'd be sixty-three, and I'd want to be the person who runs the robots, not the one they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd put twenty thousand of our savings into the farm co-op's robot fund, so members own the machines. I'd take a short course in farm robotics at the agricultural college. I'd join the campaign for community-owned automation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more about the world than about me. I'd lose some sleep over who ends up owning the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would those three years between 2028 and 2031 look like at Wren Hollow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd spend them choosing and buying robots on our own terms, before the big firms decide for us. If Wren Hollow (the community farm she works on) has to have robots, the two hundred families who buy our vegetable boxes should own them, not some company overseas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your money is secure. What exactly would keep you up at night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my kids' generation gets nothing out of it. Mia's insurance job would be gone in 2028. I'd be fine, but I'd be the lucky one, and that doesn't sit right.

say: Robots must be **owned in common** by co-ops and communities.
A **basic income** isn't a fantasy any more.
think: The **thinking side** in 2028 makes me more useful, not less.
By 2031 I want to **run the robots**, not be replaced by them.
do: Put **twenty thousand** of our savings into the co-op's robot fund.
Take a **farm robotics course** at the agricultural college.
feel: **Uneasy**, losing sleep over **who owns** the land and machines.
S2.quote: If Wren Hollow (the community farm she works on) has to have robots, the two hundred families who buy our vegetable boxes should own them, not some company overseas.
fieldNote: Her own job feels **secure enough**; her worry is ownership and fairness.
She plans to use the **three-year gap** to buy robots on members' terms.
Mia's **insurance job** is the family loss she expects first.

steps.text: Put twenty thousand of savings into the farm co-op's robot fund
Take a short farm robotics course at the agricultural college
Join the campaign for community-owned farm robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and robots by 2034. I'd be sixty-six, which is about when I'd planned to hand back my goat keys anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to do this properly, so let's set up community-owned robot schemes now. I'd say it at the members' evening and to the regional farming network. I'd write about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's comfortable. I'd likely work until I'm ready to stop. The interesting bit is helping Wren Hollow get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first years building a plan with Ines for which jobs we automate and when. I'd invest a smaller sum in the co-op's robot fund each year rather than one big lump. I'd teach other small farms in the network how to use AI for planning, for a small fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Purposeful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you charge other farms for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Setting up their sowing plans and ordering on AI, and showing them how to check it. A farmer who can lamb a ewe in the dark shouldn't be scared of a sowing app, and I can show them in an afternoon. Maybe fifty a session, enough for petrol and cake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said comfortable. Is there anything in this one that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that five years is enough for us but not for everyone. The big farms nearby could lay off pickers fast. I'd want the network to help those workers too.

I'd raise it with the **regional farming network** and write online.

The interesting part is **getting Wren Hollow ready**.

Invest a **small sum yearly** in the robot fund.
Teach small farms to plan with AI for **fifty a session**.
S3.quote: A farmer who can lamb a ewe in the dark shouldn't be scared of a sowing app, and I can show them in an afternoon.
fieldNote: Five years puts robots **past her planned stop**, removing personal risk.
She turns her skills into a **small side income** helping other farms.
Her conscience still reaches **pickers on big farms**.

steps.text: Plan with Ines which farm jobs to automate and when

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and 2039. I'd be seventy-one, probably growing tomatoes in my own polytunnel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty to build fair ownership and retraining, so there's no excuse. I'd keep saying the land and robots should serve communities. Same message, less urgency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's almost nothing, I'd have retired. I'd watch Felix and Mia more than my own job. Mia would have time to move into something people-facing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Wren Hollow until I'm ready to stop. I'd keep helping Ines with the AI planning side. I'd nudge Mia toward a claims job that involves visiting people, not just screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit wistful. I'd miss seeing the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd miss seeing them? Really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm curious, I can't help it. I spent thirty years stamping planning forms, and the most exciting part of my working life started at fifty-five with a goat called Pepper. I'd love to see what the next part looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Looking across all three fast pictures, what changes most for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just how much I get to shape it. With two years I'd be rushing to buy robots for the co-op, but with ten I could be the old woman who wrote the farm's plan.

say: A decade means **no excuse** for unfair ownership or no retraining.
The land and robots should **serve communities**.
think: I'll have **retired** before either the thinking AI or the robots land.
My daughter Mia has **time to move** into people-facing work.
do: Keep going at Wren Hollow **until I'm ready**.
Keep running the **AI planning** for Ines.
Nudge Mia toward a **visiting claims job**.
S4.quote: With two years I'd be rushing to buy robots for the co-op, but with ten I could be the old woman who wrote the farm's plan.
fieldNote: Her **curiosity** is genuine; she'd miss the change, not fear it.
Across scenarios, time decides **how much she shapes** it, not whether she's safe.
Her family worry stays with **Mia's screen job**.

steps.text: Keep working at Wren Hollow until ready to stop
Keep running the farm's AI sowing and ordering plans
Talk Mia into looking at claims jobs that involve home visits

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, not for my own job so much as who ends up owning the robots and the land. What would help is public money for co-ops and community farms to buy robots themselves, and a basic income for people whose work disappears.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd like it. And I might. If a robot milks the goats at six, I could spend the morning teaching school groups about where food comes from.
